lead: A function is a named block of steps. You write it once and call it many times. An array is one variable that holds many values in a fixed order, reached by a number called an index. An object holds many values under names called keys. These three ideas let a program grow without repeating lines. A marks table, a shopping cart and a UPI payment record are all built from them. Every browser runs JavaScript, so you meet functions, arrays and objects in page scripts, in server code and in API replies.
prereq: You need 3.1 for variables, loops and operators, because a function body is built from those statements.

blocks.text: A function is a named block of steps. Write it once, call it by name, and the same steps run again. In function average(a) { ... }, average is the function name and a is a parameter: a name in the definition that receives a value. The value you pass at the call, as in average(marks), is an argument.

A function declaration is the form above. A function expression stores a function in a variable: const average = function (a) { ... }; here the name average works only after this line. A declaration is hoisted, so the name exists before its line. A function expression is not hoisted; you must reach the assignment first.

return ends the function and sends a value back. A function with no return gives undefined, not the last value. Default parameters fill a missing argument: function area(l, w = 1) uses w = 1 when the second argument is missing or undefined. Rest parameters collect extra arguments into a real array: function sum(...nums) { /* nums is a real array */ }. Inside the body, nums is a real array.

Scope is where a name can be seen. A variable made inside a function is local to that function. Hoisting moves declarations to the top of their scope; it does not move the value assignment. Recursion is a function calling itself. For factorial, fact(n) returns n * fact(n - 1), with base fact(0) = 1. Arrow functions and classes are in 3.5.

An array stores many values in one variable, in order. A literal is let marks = [45, 72, 90, 38];. The length is marks.length, here 4. An index is a position number starting at 0. marks[0] is 45; the last index is length - 1, here 3.

push(x) adds to the end; pop() removes the end; shift() removes the start; unshift(x) adds to the start. splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) changes the original array. slice(start, end) copies a part into a new array, and end is excluded. concat joins arrays into a new array. join(sep) makes a string with sep between values. indexOf(x) gives the first index or -1; includes(x) gives true or false.

sort() without a comparator compares values as strings, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]. Use sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers. A callback is a function passed to another function. map(callback) builds a new array by applying the callback to each value. filter(callback) keeps values where the callback returns true. reduce(callback, start) folds the array into one value, such as a sum. forEach(callback) runs for each value for a side effect and returns undefined. map and filter do not change the original array.

An object stores values under names called keys. A literal is let student = { name: 'Asha', marks: 88 };. Dot access is student.name; bracket access is student['name']. Use brackets when the key has a space or is held in a variable.

A method is a function stored as a property. A nested object is an object inside another. In let school = { topper: { name: 'Asha', marks: { math: 88 } } }; the object school.topper.marks sits two levels deep, and school.topper.marks.math gives 88. Object.keys(obj) returns an array of keys; Object.values(obj) returns an array of values; Object.entries(obj) returns an array of [key, value] pairs. delete obj.key removes a property.

new Date() gives the current date and time; getFullYear() gives the year, and getMonth() gives 0 for January to 11 for December. Math.round(x) rounds to the nearest integer. x.toFixed(2) writes a number with two decimal places and returns a string, which is right for printing money or marks, such as ₹61.25.

spec.aria: The array 45, 72, 90, 38; below it the average 61.25, a filter row where 45 and 38 are greyed out giving 72, 90, and a map row giving 50, 77, 95, 43.

examples.question: marks = [45, 72, 90, 38]. (a) Write a function average(a) that adds the values with a loop and returns the mean. (b) Use filter to keep marks of 60 or more. (c) Use map to add 5 grace marks to every mark. Give all three results.
steps: Add the marks with a loop: 45 + 72 = 117; 117 + 90 = 207; 207 + 38 = 245. The sum is 245 marks.
Divide by length 4: 245 ÷ 4 = 61.25. The average is 61.25 marks.
Filter with mark >= 60: 45 is below 60, drop it; 72 is 60 or more, keep it; 90 is 60 or more, keep it; 38 is below 60, drop it. Result: [72, 90].
examples.answer: The average is 61.25 marks, the filtered array is [72, 90], and the grace-mark array is [50, 77, 95, 43].

traps: map and filter return new arrays; they do not change the original. Use push or splice when you mean to change it.
sort() without a comparator compares strings: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9], not [1, 9, 10].
A function with no return gives undefined; the last expression is not returned.
splice changes the array; slice copies. splice(1, 2) deletes two items from index 1; slice(1, 2) copies only index 1.
A default parameter runs when the argument is missing or undefined; a rest parameter collects all remaining arguments into an array.

quiz.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument.
quiz.a: A parameter is the name in the function definition, such as a in function average(a). An argument is the value passed at the call, such as marks in average(marks).
[1, 10, 9]. The values are compared as strings, so '10' comes before '9'.

quiz.q: For marks = [45, 72, 90, 38], what is marks.filter(function (m) { return m >= 60; })?
quiz.a: [72, 90]. 45 and 38 are below 60 and are dropped.

quiz.q: Why does marks.map(function (m) { return m + 5; }) not change marks?
quiz.a: map builds a new array and returns it. The original array is not changed; marks still holds [45, 72, 90, 38].

quiz.q: Given function f(a, b = 2) { return a * b; }, give f(5) and f(5, 3).
Given const s = { name: 'Asha', marks: { math: 88 } }; write two ways to read 88.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real code often works with arrays of objects from APIs, such as a list of UPI payments. Methods like map and filter appear in React rendering, and reduce powers totals on dashboards. Search for 'JavaScript array methods MDN' and 'structuredClone' to go further.
